Loading Required Packages

library(tidyverse)
library(alr4) # to access UN11 data set

Categorical Predictors

Categorical predictors are often called factors. Factors can have two levels (e.g., survived or died) or multiple levels (single, married, divorced, widowed).

We will discuss two basic uses of categorical predictors in linear regression models.

  • Parallel lines regression models produce different parallel lines for each level of the categorical variable.
  • Separate lines regression models produce separate (typically non-parallel) lines for each level of the categorical variable.

Nominal and Ordinal Variables

Categorical variables are often distinguished by whether or not they have a logical order or ranking:

  • Those that cannot be ordered logically are called nominal. For example, gender, marital status, political party.
  • Those that have an order in a sensible manner are called ordinal. For example, category of hurricane, high school class (freshman, sophomore, junior, senior).

Question 2

Create side-by-side box plots for the variable lifeExpF for each of the categories of the group variable and describe any interesting observations about the data.

Solution to Question 2

boxplot(lifeExpF ~ group, data = UN11)

  • The oecd countries generally have the largest female life expectancy and africa countries typically have the lowest.
  • Nauru and Afghanistan have unusually low female life expectancy for the other group.
  • Japan has high female life expectancy, and Turkey has low life expectancy compared to the other members of the oecd.
  • The variation of female life expectancy in oecd is smallest, but in africa is largest.
Tip

Recall when reading a box plot:

  • The thick middle line indicates the median value.
  • The box extends to the 25th and 75th percentiles. The distance between the quartiles is known as the interquartile range (IQR).
  • The whiskers generally extend to the most extreme values that are within 1.5 IQRs from the quartiles.
  • Values outside the whiskers are outliers and are indicated by a dot or star.

Indicator Variables

Suppose we wish to determine whether the categorical predictor marital status (single, cohabiting, married, divorced, and widowed) is associated with personal income. How is this type of descriptive variable entered into a quantitative model?

Dummy or indicator variables are used to include categorical predictors in a regression model.

  • An indicator function is a function that takes the value 1 if a certain property is true and 0 otherwise.
  • An indicator variable is the variable that results from applying an indicator function to each observation of a variable.

We denote indicator functions using the notation,

\[ I_S(x) = \begin{cases} 1 & \textrm{if}\;x \in S\\ 0 & \textrm{if}\;x \notin S \end{cases}. \]

Some examples of indicator functions:

  • \(I_{\rm{africa}}(\text{"Afghanistan"})= 0\)
  • \(I_{\rm{africa}}(\text{"Botswana"})= 1\)
  • \(I_{\{2,3\}}(2) = 1\).
  • \(I_{\{2,3\}}(2.5) = 0\).

In our example, group has \(d=3\) levels, \(L_1\), \(L_2\), and \(L_3\) corresponding to oecd, other, and africa, respectively. We can define three different dummy variables:

  • \(D_1\) (is country OECD?),
  • \(D_2\) (is country Other?), and
  • \(D_3\) (is country in Africa?).

Let \(c_i\) denote the value of \(C\) for observation \(i\). For example \(c_2 = \text{"other"}\). We assign values to \(D_1\), \(D_2\), and \(D_3\) using the indicator function below.

\[d_{i,j} = I_{L_j}(c_i) = \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} 1 & \mbox{if } c_i \in L_j \\ 0 & \mbox{if } c_i \notin L_j \end{array} \right.\]

Note
  • Values \(-1\) and \(1\), or \(1\) and \(2\), are sometimes used, but this is less common and more difficult to interpret.
  • The assignment labels are mostly arbitrary and do not affect the results.

One-Factor Models

If the only predictor is a factor, then the regression model is called a one-factor or one-way design. Regression coefficients for factor variables in a one-way model are often called effects.

Question 4

Let \(Y\) denote the response variable lifeExpF. What would be problematic about using the linear model proposed below?

\[Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 D_1 + \beta_2 D_2 + \beta_3 D_3 + \epsilon\]

Solution to Question 4

Since \(D_1 + D_2 + D_3 =1\), the first column (intercept) of the model matrix is linearly dependent with the last three columns. Since the model matrix is not full rank, we would not be able to invert \(X^TX\) and solve for the regression coefficients \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\).

We only need \(d-1\) dummy variables to represent \(d\) levels because the last level represented when all the other previous dummy variables are \(0\). Any of the \(d\) dummy variables could be excluded, though generally it is the first or last level.

  • R drops the first level by default.
  • The level dropped is known as the reference or baseline level.
  • In R, this method for creating the dummy variables is known as the treatment contrast.

Other possibilities for avoiding linear dependence are:

  • Drop \(\beta_0\) from the model.
  • Assume \(\sum_{i=1}^{d-1} \beta_i = 0\).
    • This is known as a sum contrast and does NOT use dummy variables.
    • Interpretation is generally more difficult.

Question 5

Using a treatment contrast with the first level of group as the reference level (oecd), what would be our model for oecd countries? What is the model for other countries? For africa countries?

\[E(\mbox{lifeExpF } \vert \mbox{ group})= \beta_0+ \beta_2 D_2+ \beta_3 D_3\].

Solution to Question 5

For the OECD group, since \(D_2=D_3=0\), we have

\[E(Y \vert \mbox{ group=oecd})= \beta_0 + \beta_2 0+ \beta_3 0= \beta_0\].

Since other implies \(D_2=1\) and \(D_3=0\), we have \[E(Y \vert \mbox{ group=other})=\beta_0 + \beta_2 1+ \beta_3 0 = \beta_0 + \beta_2.\]

Since africa implies \(D_2=0\) and \(D_3=1\), we have \[E(Y \vert \mbox{ group=africa})=\beta_0 + \beta_2 0+ \beta_3 1 = \beta_0 + \beta_3.\]

Fitting a One-Factor Model with R

R will fit a one-factor model if you:

  • Add the necessary dummy variables manually to the formula argument of lm.
  • Include the factor variable in the formula of lm (dropping the dummy variable for the first level of the factor automatically).
# First we add dummy variables to the data frame
UN11$d1 <- if_else(UN11$group == "oecd", 1, 0)
UN11$d2 <- if_else(UN11$group == "other", 1, 0)
UN11$d3 <- if_else(UN11$group == "africa", 1, 0)
# fit overparameterized model
lm(lifeExpF ~ d1 + d2 + d3, data = UN11)

Call:
lm(formula = lifeExpF ~ d1 + d2 + d3, data = UN11)

Coefficients:
(Intercept)           d1           d2           d3  
      59.77        22.67        15.55           NA  
# fit proper model
lm(lifeExpF ~ d2 + d3, data = UN11)

Call:
lm(formula = lifeExpF ~ d2 + d3, data = UN11)

Coefficients:
(Intercept)           d2           d3  
      82.45        -7.12       -22.67  
# What R will do by default
lm(lifeExpF ~ group, data = UN11)

Call:
lm(formula = lifeExpF ~ group, data = UN11)

Coefficients:
(Intercept)   groupother  groupafrica  
      82.45        -7.12       -22.67

Question 6

Compare the output from the previous three models and comment on the differences, similarities of each.

Solution to Question 6

Using the second model above with dummy variables \(D_2\) and \(D_3\), we have the following:

\(\widehat{E} (\mbox{lifeExpF }\vert\mbox{ group = oecd}) = \widehat{\beta}_0 = 82.45\),

\(\widehat{E} (\mbox{lifeExpF } \vert\mbox{ group = other}) = \widehat{\beta}_0 + \widehat{\beta}_2 = 82.45 - 7.12 = 75.33\)

\(\widehat{E} (\mbox{lifeExpF } \vert \mbox{ group = africa})= \widehat{\beta}_0 + \widehat{\beta}_3 = 82.45 - 22.67 = 59.79\).

Question 7

Interpret the practical meaning of the regression coefficients \(\widehat{\beta}_0\), \(\widehat{\beta}_2\) and \(\widehat{\beta}_3\)

Solution to Question 7

\(\beta_0\): The expected female life expectancy for OECD localities is \(82.45\) years. \(\beta_1\): The expected female life expectancy for other nations is \(75.33\) years, \(7.12\) years less than OECD localities. \(\beta_2\): The expected female life expectancy for African nations is $59.79% years, \(22.67\) years less than OECD localities

We can apply the mean function to lifeExpF separately for each group using the tapply function to check the interpretations.

tapply(UN11$lifeExpF, UN11$group, mean)
    oecd    other   africa 
82.44645 75.32674 59.77226

Factors and Quantitative Predictors

It is common to study the effect of a factor after adjusting for one or more other quantitative regressors. If we have a mixture of factors and quantitative variables in our data, it’s useful to create a scatter plot of the response versus the quantitative predictor that distinguishes the observations for each level of the categorical predictor. - This helps us assess whether the relationship between the response and quantitative regressor differs for the levels of the factor.

Question 8

Create a plot to show the relation of the response lifeExpF and predictor log(ppgdp) for each of the three country groups. What are some interesting observations/patterns you can observe in the plots?

Solution to Question 8

ggplot(UN11, aes(x = log(ppgdp), y = lifeExpF, col = group, shape = group)) + 
  geom_point()

# using base graphics
# create different colors/symbols for each group
grp_col = as.numeric(UN11$group)

# plot data, using different colors/symbols for each group
plot(lifeExpF ~ log(ppgdp), data = UN11, 
     col = grp_col, pch = grp_col)

# create the legend
legend("topleft", legend = c("oecd", "other", "africa"), col = 1:3, pch = 1:3)

We see:

  • The linear relationship between lifeExpF and log(ppgdp) is fairly weak for the African countries
  • The linear relationship is reasonably strong for the other countries
  • The linear relationship is reasonably strong for OECD countries.
  • It’s unclear whether the average rate of change between lifeExpF and log(ppgdp) (the slope) is the same for the three factor levels.
  • The average lifeExpF seems to differ vertically for the same levels of log(ppgdp) for the different factor levels.

Comparing Models

Suppose we have a response \(Y\), a quantitative regressor \(X\), and a two-level factor variable represented by a single dummy variable \(D\):

Note

The model described extends naturally when the factor has more than 2 levels (as with our group predictor).

\[D = \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} 0 & \mbox{for the reference level} \\ 1 & \mbox{for the treatment level} \end{array} \right.\]

Consider several possible regression models.

A Simple Linear Regression Model

A simple linear regression model with one quantitative predictor will produce the same, single regression line for all levels of the categorical variable (combined), \(Y= \beta_0 + \beta_1 X + \epsilon\).

Question 9

Enter code to fit a simple linear model with log(ppgdp) as the regressor and lifeExpF as the response. Store the output of the linear model to an object called lmods (s is for simple). Add this line to the scatter plot you created in Question 8

Solution to Question 9

lmods <- lm(lifeExpF ~  log(ppgdp), data = UN11)
summary(lmods)

lm(formula = lifeExpF ~ log(ppgdp), data = UN11)

A One-Way Model

We looked at a one-way model in Question 7 and Question 8. This model uses only a factor predictor but no quantitative predictor, \(Y= \beta_0 + \beta_2 D + \epsilon\).

lmodo <- lm(lifeExpF ~  group, data = UN11)
summary(lmodo)

Call:
lm(formula = lifeExpF ~ group, data = UN11)

Residuals:
     Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
-25.8367  -3.3045   0.3635   2.7183  18.2277

Main Effects or Parallel Lines Model

Main effects or parallel lines models create separate regression lines for each group, each having the same slope, \(Y= \beta_0+ \beta_1 X+ \beta_2 D + \epsilon\).

  • \(\beta_2\) represents the vertical distance between the regression lines (the effect of the treatment).

Question 11

Find formulas for each of the parallel lines in your model from Question 10.

Solution to Question 11

In general, we have

\[\begin{align} \widehat{\mbox{lifeExpF}} =& \widehat{\mbox{E}}(\mbox{lifeExpF} \vert \mbox{ppgdp}, \mbox{group})\\ &= 49.529 + 3.177 \log{(\mbox{ppgdp})} -1.535 D_2 - 12.17 D_3 \end{align}\]

If the group is oecd, then \(D_2=0\) and \(D_3=0\) giving

\[\begin{align} \widehat{\mbox{lifeExpF}} &= \widehat{\mbox{E}}(\mbox{lifeExpF} \vert \mbox{ppgdp}=x, \mbox{group=oecd})\\ &= 49.529 + 3.177 \log{(\mbox{ppgdp})} \end{align}\]

If the group is other, then \(D_2=1\) and \(D_3=0\) giving

\[\begin{align} \widehat{\mbox{lifeExpF}} =& \widehat{\mbox{E}}(\mbox{lifeExpF} \vert \mbox{ppgdp}, \mbox{group=other})\\ &= 47.994 + 3.177 \log{(\mbox{ppgdp})} \end{align}\]

If the group is africa, then \(D_2=0\) and \(D_3=1\) giving

\[\begin{align} \widehat{\mbox{lifeExpF}} =& \widehat{\mbox{E}}(\mbox{lifeExpF} \vert \mbox{ppgdp}, \mbox{group=afric})\\ &= 37.359 + 3.177 \log{(\mbox{ppgdp})} \end{align}\]

Plotting Parallel Lines Model

UN11 <- UN11 |>
  mutate(life_fitted = predict(lmodp))
# add a line geom for each model
ggplot(UN11, aes(x = log(ppgdp), y = lifeExpF)) +
  geom_point(aes(shape = group, color = group)) +
  geom_line(aes(x = log(ppgdp), y = life_fitted, color = group))

Interaction Model

Interaction or separate lines model plot separate lines for each group that have different slopes, \(Y= \beta_0+ \beta_1 X+ \beta_2 D+ \beta_3 XD + \epsilon\).

In R, we can use the syntax y ~ x + u + x:u or y ~ x*u

  • x:d means the interaction between x and d.
  • x*d means the cross between x and d (x, d, and the interaction between x and d).

\[\begin{aligned} \widehat{\mbox{lifeExpF}} &= \widehat{E}(\mbox{lifeExpF} \vert \mbox{ppgdp}=x, \mbox{group=africa})\\ &= 59.21 + 2.24 \log{(x)} -22.98 +1.09 \log{(x)}\\ &= 36.23 + 5.41 \log{(x)} \end{aligned}\]

Question 15

Interpret each coefficient in your separate lines models from Question 13.

Solution to Question 15

For oecd countries: - For every \(1\%\) increase in an OECD country’s GDP per capita, the life expectancy of females is predicted to increase by about \(0.0224\) years, on average. - If an OECD’s country has GDP per capita equal to \(\$1\), the life expectancy of females is predicted to be 59 years.

For other countries: - For every \(1\%\) increase in an other country’s GDP per capita, the life expectancy of females is predicted to increase by about \(0.0317\) years, on average. - If an other country has GDP per capita equal to \(\$1\), the life expectancy of females is predicted to be 48 years.

For africa countries: - For every \(1\%\) increase in an African country’s GDP per capita, the life expectancy of females is predicted to increase by about \(0.0541\) years, on average. - If an African country has GDP per capita equal to \(\$1\), the life expectancy of females is predicted to be 36 years.

Comparing slopes in the the three models, we can see that if a country increases its GDP per capita by \(1\%\), then the corresponding increase in life expectancy of females is greatest in Africa, second greatest in the other group, and least for OECD countries.

Note

The interpretation of the intercept terms for an interaction model can be problematic in practice because the size difference between the coefficients might not represent a typical difference if the range of the quantitative regressor doesn’t include zero.

Appendix A: Multiple Linear Regression Models

The Basic Model

\[Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_1 + \beta_2 X_2 + \ldots + \beta_{p-1} X_{p-1} + \epsilon .\]

Error Assumptions

  1. The errors \(\epsilon_i\) have mean zero, \(E(\epsilon_i) = 0\) for all \(i\).
  2. The errors are normally distributed.
  3. The errors all have the same, constant variance (homoscedascity).
  4. The errors are uncorrelated.
  5. Collinearity No combination of predictors has a perfect association.

We can restate error assumptions (1)-(4) as:

\[\large \epsilon_i \sim N(0, \sigma^2) \qquad \text{and} \qquad \text{Cov}(\epsilon_i, \epsilon_j) = 0 \ \ \text{ if } i \ne j.\]

The OLS Estimator

\[\boldsymbol{\hat{\beta}} = \left( \mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X} \right)^{-1} \mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{y}\] We can express solution to OLS equivalently as the solution to a matrix equation

\[\mathbf{X} \boldsymbol{\hat{\beta}} = \mathbf{H} \mathbf{y} , \qquad \mathbf{R} \boldsymbol{\hat{\beta}} = \mathbf{Q}^T \mathbf{y} , \quad \text{or} \quad \boldsymbol{\hat{\beta}} = \mathbf{V} \mathbf{\Sigma}^{-1} \mathbf{U}^T \mathbf{y} .\]

Measurements of Association

  • Covariance measures how strong is the dependence between two variables

\[\mbox{Cov}(X,Y) = E\bigg( (X-\mu_X)(Y-\mu_Y) \bigg) . \]

  • The correlation coefficient is scaled measure of the relation between \(X\) and \(Y\)

\[\rho_{X,Y} = \frac{\mbox{Cov}(X,Y)}{\sigma_X \cdot \sigma_Y} .\]

  • \(R^2\), the coefficient of determination is the percentage of variance in the response explained by the model

\[R^2=1- \frac{\sum (Y_i - \widehat{Y}_i)^2}{\sum (Y_i - \overline{Y})^2} =1- \frac{\mbox{RSS}}{\mbox{TSS}}= \frac{\mbox{SS}_{\rm reg}} {\mbox{TSS}} = \mbox{Cor}^2(\mathbf{y}, \hat{\mathbf{y}}) .\]

  • \(\mbox{RSS} = \sum (Y_i - \widehat{Y}_i)^2\) is the Residual Sum of Squares (RSS) (variation that is not explained by model).
  • \(\mbox{TSS} = \sum (Y_i - \overline{Y})^2\) is the Total Sum of Squares correct for the mean (TSS) (total variation in the response).
  • \(\mbox{SS}_{\rm reg} = \sum (\widehat{Y}_i - \overline{Y})^2 = \mbox{TSS} - \mbox{RSS}\) is the regression sum of squares (variation that is explained by model).

\[\mbox{TSS} = \mbox{RSS} + \mbox{SS}_{\rm reg} .\]

Appendix B: Useful Functions with lm()

Some useful commands working with lm:

  • coef(lmod) returns the values of the regression coefficients.
  • x <- model.matrix( ~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4, data = data.frame) creates matrix \(\mathbf{X}\).
  • y <- data.frame$response_var creates vector of observed values of \(\mathbf{y}\).
  • residuals(lmod) vector of residuals \(\hat{\boldsymbol\epsilon}\).
  • deviance(lmod) computes the RSS of the linear model.
  • df.residual(lmod) computes the degrees of freedom \(n-p\).
  • sigma(lmod) computes the estimate for the standard error \(\hat{\sigma}\).
  • summary(lmod)$r.squared gives \(R^2\) value.
  • summary(lmod)$adj.r.squared gives the adjusted \(R^2\) value.
  • names(lmod) lists quantities we can extract from the lmod.
  • vcov(lmod) estimated covariance matrix of the regression coefficients.

Appendix C: Collinearity and Regression

Suppose we want to construct a one-factor model where the categorical variable has \(d\) levels and we include \(d\) dummy variables (one for each level instead of \(d-1\) by dropping the first dummy variable) and an intercept term. Why is this problematic?

Consider our example with UN11 data where we constructed a model for predicting the response lifeExpF based on the level of the categorical variable group.

# create dummy variables
library(alr4)
data(UN11)
UN11 <- transform(UN11, 
          d1 = ifelse(group == "oecd", 1, 0),
          d2 = ifelse(group == "other", 1, 0),
          d3 = ifelse(group == "africa", 1, 0))
  • Each observation is in exactly one group (either oecd, other, or africa).
  • One of the dummy variables is 1 and the other two are 0.
  • Thus, for each observation, \(d_1 + d_2 + d_3 = 1\).
# construct model matrix
x <- model.matrix(~ d1 + d2 + d3, data = UN11)
head(x)

Algeria               1  0  0  1
Angola                1  0  0  1
Anguilla              1  0  1  0
Argentina             1  0  1  0

We can see the columns are linearly dependent since \(\text{intercept} = d_1 + d_2 + d_3\).

Identifiability

The least squares estimator is the solution to the matrix equation \(\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X} \boldsymbol{\hat{\beta}} = \mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{y}\), where \(\mathbf{X}\) is the \(n \times p\) model (or design) matrix.

Unidentifiability will occur when \(X\) is not full rank} (the columns of \(X\) are linearly dependent).

  • If \(\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X}\) cannot be inverted, there is no unique solution to the equation and \(\boldsymbol{\hat{\beta}}\) is unidentifiable.
  • Unidentifiable means that different parameter values can result in the same model (predictions).
Note

Problems with unidentifiability are rare for observational data, but more common with experiments. Here are some examples for observational data:

  • A person’s weight is measured and entered in both pounds and kilos. One is just a multiple of the other.
  • We record the number of years of pre-university education, university education, and total education. There is a perfect linear relationship between these variables.
  • We have more variables than observations.
    • When \(p=n\) we have a saturated model, and we may be able to estimate some of the parameters.
    • When \(p>n\), we have a supersaturated model, and cannot uniquely estimate parameters.
  • Removing one (or more) of the linearly dependent columns should correct the problem!
  • R tries to fit the largest identifiable model by removing variables in reverse order of appearance in the model formula.
  • We can usually identify the source of linear dependence with a little thought, or if necessary, using linear algebra to understand the structure of of the matrix \(\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X}\).

Orthogonality

Let \(\mathbf{X}_j\) denote the vector of observed values for regressor \(X_j\). Vectors \(\mathbf{X}_i\) and \(\mathbf{X}_j\) are orthogonal if \(X_i^T X_j=0\).

It is generally good for regressors to be orthogonal, especially when designing experiments, because orthogonality ensures that their association with the response variable can be estimated independently from each other. This property leads to stable parameter estimates that are easy to interpret since the addition or removal of orthogonal regressors does not change the other coefficient estimates.

If a regressor \(\mathbf{X}_i\) is orthogonal to another regressor (and all other regressors already in the model):

  • It’s addition or deletion from the fitted model will not change the estimated regression coefficients for the other regressors.
  • The values of \(\mathbf{X}_i\) have no effect on the relation between all other regressors and the prediction.
  • Removing the regressor does effect the estimates standard error a little bit.

Example: Odor Data

The odor data set from the faraway package contains data from an experiment to determine the effects of temperature (temp), gas/liquid ratio (gas), and packing height (pack) in reducing unpleasant odor of a chemical product.

data(odor, package = "faraway")
head(odor)
  odor temp gas pack
1   66   -1  -1    0
2   39    1  -1    0
3   43   -1   1    0
4   49    1   1    0

6   17    1   0   -1
# predictors are pairwise orthogonal
crossprod(odor$temp, odor$gas)
     [,1]
[1,]    0
crossprod(odor$temp, odor$pack)
     [,1]
[1,]    0
crossprod(odor$pack, odor$gas)
     [,1]
[1,]    0
# construct model matrix
x_odor <- model.matrix(~ temp + gas + pack, 
                  data = odor)
crossprod(x_odor) # matrix crossproduct X^T X
            (Intercept) temp gas pack
(Intercept)          15    0   0    0
temp                  0    8   0    0
gas                   0    0   8    0
pack                  0    0   0    8
# model using all three predictors and intercept
odor_lmod1 <- lm(odor ~ temp + gas + pack, data = odor)
coef(odor_lmod1)
(Intercept)        temp         gas        pack 
     15.200     -12.125     -17.000     -21.375 
# remove the intercept from the model
odor_lmod2 <- lm(odor ~ temp + gas + pack + 0, data = odor)
coef(odor_lmod2)
   temp     gas    pack 
-12.125 -17.000 -21.375 
# add intercept back but now remove pack as predictor
odor_lmod3 <- lm(odor ~ temp + gas, data = odor)
coef(odor_lmod3)
(Intercept)        temp         gas 
     15.200     -12.125     -17.000
